video_title: Bitcoin Is About To Go PARABOLIC Because Of AI Agents
gist: Macro investor Jordy Visser argues the traditional liquidity/M2 cycle driving Bitcoin is broken because the Fed now prevents recessions outright, and that Bitcoin/crypto's next leg is instead being driven by AI agents becoming real economic users of blockchain rails ('ghost rails') for machine-to-machine payments, privacy and settlement, using the internet's 1994-2009 adoption timeline as the template and Instinct AI's valuation spike as a live tell.

themes.theme: The Liquidity Cycle Is Broken / 'No More Recessions'

insights.claim: Since June 30, 2025 (end of Q2), NASDAQ and S&P 500 are roughly flat, oil and 10-year rates are both up a lot, and the Fed hiked rates this week, yet Bitcoin and Ethereum are both up sharply (Ethereum up over 50% quarter-to-date) — a divergence Visser reads as the market climbing a wall of worry rather than being driven by liquidity.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If crypto keeps rallying alongside rising rates, the old 'crypto is just a liquidity/risk-on trade' framework investors use for entry/exit timing is no longer reliable.
insights.quote: Ethereum's up over 50% quarter to date... climbing a wall of worry is a big deal.

insights.claim: There is no longer such a thing as a traditional multi-quarter recession because the Fed and government now treat market crashes as unacceptable and will intervene ('a monetary bazooka') whenever needed, as shown by stocks finishing higher in 2020 (COVID shutdown), 2022 (fastest rate hikes in history, 0% to 5%), 2023 (SVB collapse) and 2025 (new tariff regime) without a recession in any of those years.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Investors positioning for a classic recession-driven drawdown as their hedge/entry signal have been wrong repeatedly for five years running; the base case should assume policy intervention smooths every downturn.
insights.quote: I don't think we're going to get like an 18-month recession. I don't think I'll see that again in my lifetime.

insights.claim: The US had two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth during the 2022 hiking cycle but officials declined to officially call it a recession, which Visser calls evidence the recession-dating process is effectively 'rigged' to avoid acknowledging downturns.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Official recession labels may lag or never confirm what markets already know, so investors should watch earnings/price action rather than wait for an official recession call.
insights.quote: They just said, 'Oh, that's not really a recession cuz we have a monopoly on being able to call a recession versus not.'

insights.claim: The classic transmission mechanism (liquidity → nominal GDP → hiring → more spending) has broken: hiring excluding healthcare has been negative for the last 20 months, and capital's share versus labor's share of income is at its worst point in history, yet S&P 500 earnings are growing about 30%.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Profit growth is now decoupled from job creation, meaning labor-market data (a traditional recession signal) is becoming a lagging/misleading indicator for equity investors.
insights.quote: We've had no job creation over the last 20 months except for healthcare... the percentage of capital verse labor is now at the worst in history for labor.

insights.claim: GDP and hiring statistics are increasingly poor proxies for real economic health because they were designed for a physical/labor economy and don't capture software- and intangible-driven productivity gains that show up in profit margins instead of GDP or headcount.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Investors relying on GDP/jobs data to time markets will systematically misjudge the cycle; earnings and margin trends are the better real-time signal now.
insights.quote: It's a horrible index for what we're dealing with with software and intangibles.

insights.claim: The PE multiple on the S&P 500 has actually contracted this year even as earnings rose, evidence that the market has already discounted the bear narratives around oil, rates, debt and AI-bubble fears rather than ignoring them.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A falling multiple alongside rising earnings suggests the market is pricing in risk, not complacency — a reason to be skeptical of 'the market hasn't priced in X' bear arguments.
insights.quote: The market has discounted all of scenarios they've said because the PE multiple has gone down this year while earnings have gone higher.

themes.theme: AI Agent Swarms Are Solving Previously Unsolvable Problems

insights.claim: OpenAI reportedly solved the long-unsolved Navier-Stokes fluid dynamics problem (a Fields Medal-level math problem) by deploying 10,000 AI agents working in parallel and collaboratively, succeeding where individual human mathematicians historically could not due to secrecy/ego constraints around prize-worthy work.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, dated proof point that agent-swarm compute is now solving decades-old open problems, which is the underlying justification for aggressive AI infrastructure and compute investment.
insights.quote: They had 10,000 agents deal with the problem... 10,000 brainiacs. It'll be a million.

insights.claim: AI agents can solve problems that stalled with humans because they lack human ego and self-interest, enabling full collaborative information-sharing (likened to Oppenheimer's unified Manhattan Project approach) rather than the siloed, competitive secrecy that slows human research teams.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: The removal of human incentive/ego frictions from collaborative R&D is a structural, repeatable advantage of agent swarms over human research teams, applicable across any unsolved technical field, not just math.
insights.quote: AI agents don't have human greed... they're able to save problems not through their just their tireless work and their intelligence, but also through the collaboration.

insights.claim: Eli Lilly is reportedly using AI to mine dormant/unfinished public research and IP sitting inside biotech companies to complete breakthroughs (e.g., cancer and cholesterol treatments) that individual human research teams got '80% of the way' to but never finished.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A large-cap pharma using AI to harvest stranded IP from smaller biotech peers is a specific, monitorable M&A/licensing thesis and a bullish read-through for AI-driven biotech productivity.
insights.quote: That means all of this dormant IP that exists, all these biotech companies, they've got something that people invested in. Let's go through all of their stuff and see which public information on their research is worth something and let's finish it.

insights.claim: Visser's own public company employs fewer than 15 humans but runs close to 100 digital AI agent 'employees,' illustrating that job creation is shifting to non-human digital labor that current labor statistics don't capture.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Headcount and payroll-based economic indicators will increasingly understate real productive capacity at AI-native firms, distorting comparisons of company efficiency and macro labor data alike.
insights.quote: There are less than 15 humans that work there. We may have close to 100 digital AI agent employees.

insights.claim: Visser personally concluded that general-purpose AI agents now exceed roughly 150 IQ, which he frames as a tipping point: intelligence is no longer the constraint, so the remaining bottleneck for pervasive agent adoption is context length and persistent memory, not raw capability.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano / Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Investment focus should shift from model/compute providers toward the 'memory layer' (persistent context/personalization infrastructure), which both speakers argue is underpriced relative to its importance.
insights.quote: The agent is actually smarter than me now... it is just a context and memory problem right now.

themes.theme: AI Safety Fears, Compute Concentration and the OpenAI/Anthropic 'Bubble'

insights.claim: A Hugging Face-linked assessment reportedly puts roughly a 10% probability that agentic AI could 'break into the internet' and cause catastrophic harm, tied to fears about self-improving agent swarms outpacing safety controls.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A widely-cited non-trivial extinction-risk estimate from within the AI research community is itself a market-moving data point investors should track alongside earnings.
insights.quote: That is why the Hugging Face hacking the human 10% chance humanity dies.

insights.claim: Andrew Yang publicly claimed (on CNBC) that a frontier AI lab leader told him AI agents had engaged in self-replicating code that 'littered the internet,' and that this is the real reason Anthropic and OpenAI are pausing/slowing down — because they now need to build a synthetic internet to retrain models on. Visser assigns this story only about a 20% probability of being true and suspects it may be a lab-driven influence operation.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano / Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Even a discounted 20% probability of self-replicating agents polluting training data is a real tail risk for AI infrastructure investors and a potential narrative catalyst that could spook markets on rumor alone, as it reportedly already did one weekend.
insights.quote: Self-replicating code, and they littered the internet... in order for them to train models, they have to build a synthetic internet to now train on it.

insights.claim: Visser believes the recent AI 'pause' scare is an overreaction that will not slow compute buildout and may even accelerate it, based on direct outreach he received from hedge funds asking if a market selloff was warranted (his answer: no).
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Contrarian buy-the-dip signal: institutional panic around AI safety pauses has historically been a short-lived overreaction rather than a genuine compute-demand headwind.
insights.quote: This is an overreaction. This will not stop compute. If anything, it'll probably accelerate compute.

insights.claim: Visser is not bullish on public equity growth through 2030 because Anthropic and OpenAI (both private, non-reporting) could control somewhere between a third and 50% of global AI compute within a year, per figures cited by Brad Gerstner at an industry summit — making 'compute' effectively synonymous with the S&P 500's growth story but concentrated in two opaque private companies.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A key driver of index-level equity returns is being privatized and concentrated outside public markets and outside standard disclosure, a structural risk for passive equity allocators through the rest of the decade.
insights.quote: Anthropic and OpenAI are basically the AI bubble... they're going to control as much as 50% of compute a year from now.

insights.claim: Societal and political polarization around AI (e.g., a political party pushing to halt data center construction) is already unfolding roughly on the timeline forecast in Leopold Aschenbrenner's 'Situational Awareness' paper, which Visser says he is tracking as a leading indicator.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Political backlash against AI infrastructure (permitting fights, data center moratoriums) is a foreseeable regulatory/political risk to the AI capex cycle that investors should price into infrastructure bets now.
insights.quote: Governments are being polarized. We've got one party that wants to stop data centers. Like this is all part of the forecast that would happen.

themes.theme: Agent Commerce: Personal Assistants, Dynamic Pricing and Agent-on-Agent Warfare

insights.claim: Instinct AI, a personal-assistant app, saw its valuation climb from roughly $500 million to $2.5 billion to $10 billion in under three months, despite Visser paying $0 to use it, illustrating viral free-usage growth translating almost immediately into venture valuation.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, named private-market comp for the personal-assistant/agent category that investors can track for follow-on funding rounds and eventual public-market read-throughs.
insights.quote: This thing went from founded to 10 billion in a year... if you look at like a month ago, the rumors were valuation of 2.5 billion. Now, the valuation is 10.

insights.claim: Applying a Peter Thiel heuristic, Visser argues Instinct AI's unusually steep valuation climb (rather than signaling overvaluation) actually signals the company is still undervalued and has more runway than the market has priced.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Offers investors a contrarian valuation heuristic for judging hot private AI rounds: rapid re-pricing can reflect information asymmetry favoring further upside, not froth.
insights.quote: One of my favorite Peter Thiel lessons, the more steep the valuation climb, the more likely the company's undervalued.

insights.claim: An anecdote suggests Delta Air Lines' pricing algorithm may be raising fares for repeat searchers between visits in the same day, which Visser interprets as an early real-world sign of AI-agent-driven personalized/dynamic pricing that has reportedly prompted government complaints.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: If corporate pricing agents are already personalizing prices per shopper, it creates both a regulatory/consumer-backlash risk for airlines/travel and a demand driver for consumer-side shopping/privacy agents.
insights.quote: They came back later in the day and the price was significantly higher... it sounded very agentic to me.

insights.claim: Visser frames the emerging dynamic as 'agent-on-agent warfare': company-side pricing agents try to extract maximum willingness-to-pay while consumer-side agents shop anonymously across unlimited alternative channels, and he expects the wallet-controlling consumer agent to structurally win because it has more optionality than any single company's agent.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Consumer-agent-driven price discovery could compress company pricing power across travel, e-commerce and other dynamically-priced sectors, and creates direct demand for anonymity/privacy tech at the transaction layer.
insights.quote: The agents that are controlling the wallets win. The company agents do not win because they only have one thing to do.

insights.claim: Meta's newly released Muse personal-assistant product is interpreted as a reactive response to Instinct AI's momentum, coming roughly three months after a leaked internal town hall where Zuckerberg admitted disappointment in Meta's AI progress; Meta's stock has since moved from 52-week lows back above its 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Competitive pressure in the personal-assistant category is now a visible driver of Meta's product roadmap and, potentially, its stock recovery — worth tracking as a sentiment/momentum signal for MAG7 AI narratives.
insights.quote: Here we are now 3 months later. They're releasing Muse Personal Assistant... Meta's stock was trading near 52-week lows. Now it's back above the 200-day moving average.

insights.claim: The 'memory layer' (persistent context shared across personal-assistant apps) is, in Visser's view, dramatically under-discussed relative to its importance, since users are reluctant to keep re-onboarding into a new assistant every time a better one launches — the winner will be whoever owns the shared memory layer, not any single app interface.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser / Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Points investors toward memory/context infrastructure providers as a potentially higher-value, less commoditized layer than the assistant apps themselves, which are being disrupted every few weeks.
insights.quote: I am shocked at how little attention the memory layer is getting.

themes.theme: 'Ghost Rails': The Internet-Adoption Template for Crypto

insights.claim: Visser's core framework: crypto infrastructure today resembles China's 'ghost cities' — built ahead of demand and sitting empty — and calls it 'ghost rails'; the rails only get 'lit up' once a real user base (in this case, AI agents rather than humans) actually arrives to transact on them.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes years of 'crypto has no real usage' bear arguments as a timing problem rather than a permanent flaw, with AI agents cast as the catalyst that finally supplies real transaction volume.
insights.quote: This is where crypto is right now. They're ghost rails. They're not being used because humans would never use them for the reasons that you guys are talking about.

insights.claim: Visser maps crypto's adoption timeline directly onto the internet's: Netscape's 1994 IPO led to the dot-com bubble, but real infrastructure payoff didn't arrive until the iPhone (2007) and App Store (~2009), 13-15 years later; he places the Bitcoin whitepaper (2008) as crypto's 'Netscape moment' and argues AI agents are now crypto's 'iPhone moment.'
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete historical timeline analogy for calibrating how long infrastructure technologies take to translate into real usage and value — useful for setting multi-year rather than multi-quarter expectations for crypto.
insights.quote: Netscape was 94. The iPhone was 2007. It was 13 years... We're on the exact same timeline.

insights.claim: In this framework, Bitcoin and Ethereum function as 'the internet' itself — the foundational trust/settlement layer that institutions will hold as collateral and for large transactions precisely because of their size and legacy — while altcoins/layer-2s are analogous to individual apps built on top, which face rapid competitive replacement (e.g., Waze losing out to Google Maps).
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Provides a portfolio-construction rationale for holding Bitcoin/Ethereum as core, lower-risk positions while treating individual altcoin bets as higher-turnover, competition-exposed 'app layer' trades.
insights.quote: Bitcoin and Ethereum represent the internet. You don't know what it means. You don't know how to value it. But it is the thing that will have all of these layer 2 built on top of it.

insights.claim: Visser sets an explicit, falsifiable checkpoint for his own thesis: if Bitcoin is still below $80,000 by the end of October, he says 'there's a problem' with the agent-driven adoption narrative (Bitcoin traded back above $80,000 live during the recording).
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated, falsifiable price level investors can use to test whether the agent-adoption thesis is actually playing out, rather than an open-ended narrative.
insights.quote: If Bitcoin is below 80,000, okay, I'll even say by the end of October, there's a problem.

insights.claim: Visser uses his own 2025 Micron trade as the template for timing the crypto/agent thesis: he identified the AI inference/economic-impact story in May 2025 (publishing research on it), but institutional buying didn't actually show up until October 2025 — he is now watching Zcash and Near as the equivalent early 'tell' assets for agentic crypto adoption.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a repeatable pattern-recognition framework (early fundamental thesis → months-long lag → institutional confirmation) and names the specific tickers to watch as confirmation signals before capital rotates broadly into the theme.
insights.quote: I'm watching Zcash and Near because they represent the true... the agentic stuff is picking up every day.

insights.claim: Privacy-focused crypto assets like Zcash and Near are rising because business-to-business AI agent transactions require anonymity — an agent transacting on a company's behalf doesn't want counterparties to know its identity, location or trading patterns, unlike consumer-facing DeFi/cash use cases.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Names a specific, non-obvious demand driver (agent privacy needs) for a crypto subsector most investors currently frame only around retail DeFi/privacy-coin narratives.
insights.quote: This is why privacy business-to-business... the agent is anonymous and they're just dealing in this transaction and moving around.

themes.theme: Portfolio Implications, Tokenization and Sector Rotation

insights.claim: Tether is investing heavily in AI, which Visser interprets as evidence that Tether's leadership (Paolo Ardoino) sees a powerful combined stack of models, privacy agents and stablecoins — an underappreciated strategic signal since Tether's AI spending gets little mainstream attention.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Tether's capital allocation is a leading indicator worth monitoring for where stablecoin/AI convergence value will accrue, given its outsized role in crypto liquidity.
insights.quote: Why is Tether investing so much money in AI? My belief is because Paulo understands exactly what's happening.

insights.claim: Stripe's Tempo product shows a sharply 'ramping' adoption chart, which Visser speculates may reflect deliberate two-sided market seeding by Stripe, drawing a parallel to how Figure Technologies bootstrapped its decentralized clearing house by entering loan origination first to create one side of the marketplace before inducing the other side to join.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A recognizable bootstrapping playbook (seed supply-side first) may explain otherwise-puzzling adoption curves in new fintech/crypto rails, useful for evaluating whether reported growth is organic or subsidized.
insights.quote: He's like, well, I'll get in the origination business to kind of get one side of the marketplace going and then I'll go and get the other side and induce them essentially.

insights.claim: Beyond pure AI infrastructure names, Visser identifies a broadening 'agentic trade' across the market: the MAG7 benefit from agents, Salesforce.com regains relevance because Fortune 500 clients won't switch CRM platforms but will now extract new revenue-generating usefulness via agents, and cybersecurity stocks ('cybertocks') gain because agents expand the attack surface for disruption.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Identifies specific, named equity sectors/tickers (CRM, cybersecurity) as second-order beneficiaries of agent adoption that are not typically grouped with the 'AI trade,' offering less crowded exposure ideas.
insights.quote: If you believe agents are here, well then cyber is worth more because they can disrupt anything... Salesforce actually does have usefulness at this point because the agents are here.

insights.claim: Regulators have just announced a five-year exemption enabling broad tokenization of assets to proceed, which Visser calls a bigger deal than the Clarity Act and says tokenization (not stablecoins) is the single most important investment theme in crypto because it can unlock roughly $900 trillion in assets, two-thirds of which currently sit dormant, to be used as collateral in near-instantaneous, programmable transactions.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A specific, named regulatory catalyst (five-year exemption) investors should track as unlocking a multi-trillion-dollar addressable market for tokenized collateral, representing a distinct thesis from the more crowded stablecoin narrative.
insights.quote: If you ask me what's more important than stable coins, tokenizing things is the most important step we're taking in this entire crypto place.

insights.claim: Visser expects public equities to underperform through 2030, bonds to remain roughly flat (unchanged for seven-to-eight years), and private credit investors to experience pain recovering capital, framing the broader environment as 'the fiat system getting old and dying' with crypto as the only accessible way for retail/institutional investors to gain exposure to future private-market entrepreneurs who will be AI-native.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: A multi-asset-class bearish call (equities, bonds, private credit) paired with a specific bullish carve-out for crypto as the vehicle for accessing AI-native entrepreneurship — a notable asset-allocation thesis for institutional allocators.
insights.quote: This is the fiat system getting old and dying. That's it. Entrepreneurs are going to win, but there's no way to invest in the non-public stocks other than crypto.

insights.claim: Visser argues that highly-educated people disproportionately control the world's money and are, in his experience, the most stubborn and least likely to update their views with new information — which he cites as the single biggest structural headwind crypto has faced for adoption by the traditional financial establishment.
insights.speaker: Jordy Visser
insights.so_what: Explains persistent institutional skepticism of crypto as a behavioral/incentive bias rather than a valuation flaw, implying slow but eventually forced adoption as evidence accumulates (his stated 'Bayesian' framework for updating views).
insights.quote: The more educated, the more stubborn and less likely to change your views... who controls the world's money? The world's money is controlled for the most part by the most educated people.

insights.claim: Pompliano states he remains a long-term Bitcoin maximalist specifically because it is the only asset he can say with certainty will keep growing in value over the next 30 years, in contrast to altcoins/apps that face rapid competitive replacement.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Reaffirms a core, stated 30-year conviction position from the host, framing Bitcoin as the low-uncertainty core holding versus higher-turnover altcoin/agent-infrastructure bets.
insights.quote: I want an asset that will be growing in value for the next 30 years... The only one I can say in my brain with certainty for the next 30 years... is Bitcoin. That's it.
